items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a statement that can be tested by collecting and analysing data, which may be accepted or rejected”.
items.answer: Hypothesis
items.markingKey: Hypothesis: a statement that can be tested by collecting and analysing data, which may be accepted or rejected. [1]

items.stem: Explain why a hypothesis must be testable.
items.answer: It must name measurable variables so that data can be collected and analysed to show clearly whether it is supported or rejected.
items.markingKey: 1 mark measurable variables; 1 mark accept/reject [2]

items.stem: Explain why investigators carry out a risk assessment before fieldwork.
items.answer: To identify hazards (traffic, water, weather, strangers) and plan how to reduce them so that students are safe.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identify hazards; 1 mark reduce risk [2]

items.stem: Students are investigating whether pedestrian numbers decrease with distance from the centre of the CBD of Karachi. Describe and justify a suitable sampling strategy.
items.answer: Systematic sampling: sites every 100 m along a transect from the centre, which gives an even, unbiased spread of data that can be compared.
items.markingKey: 1 mark strategy; 1 mark justification [2]

items.stem: Students are investigating how microclimate varies around their school in Mexico City. (a) Describe a method of collecting primary data to test the hypothesis. (b) Suggest one source of secondary data that would help the investigation.
items.answer: (a) Measuring air temperature with a digital thermometer and wind speed with a hand-held anemometer at the same height at each site. (b) Maps, census or council data, Environment Agency or weather records, previous studies, websites or old photographs.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark method; 1 mark detail (how/where/when) [2] (b) [1]

items.stem: Students are investigating how environmental quality varies between different residential areas of Accra. Jonas’s group has one day for fieldwork and their hypothesis is “Environmental quality is higher in the suburbs than in the inner city.” (a) Explain why a pilot study would be useful. (b) Explain how the group could make sure their results are reliable.
items.answer: (a) To check that methods work, that questions or recording sheets are clear, and how long each site takes, so the day is used efficiently. (b) Repeat measurements and take means, use the same equipment and times at each site, use a large enough sample, and have the same person record each measurement.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each up to [2] (b) 1 mark each up to [3]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a statement that there is no relationship or difference between the variables being studied”.
items.answer: Null hypothesis
items.markingKey: Null hypothesis: a statement that there is no relationship or difference between the variables being studied. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “A hypothesis that is rejected means the investigation has failed.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Rejecting a hypothesis is a valid conclusion; the evidence still tells us something about the area.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “choosing sample points so that every member of the population has an equal chance of being selected, for example using random numbers”.
items.answer: Random sampling
items.markingKey: Random sampling: choosing sample points so that every member of the population has an equal chance of being selected, for example using random numbers. [1]

items.stem: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of random sampling.
items.answer: Advantage: avoids bias because every point has an equal chance. Disadvantage: may miss important areas or give an uneven spread, and some points may be inaccessible.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Explain how to measure the width and depth of a river.
items.answer: Stretch a tape across the river from water edge to water edge to measure width; measure depth with a metre rule at equal intervals (e.g. every 50 cm) across the channel and calculate the mean.
items.markingKey: 1 mark width; 1 mark depth at intervals; 1 mark mean [3]

items.stem: Students measured a river at one site. Width = 3.4 m. Depths (cm) at equal intervals from bank to bank: 0, 22, 48, 57, 0. A float took 28.7, 23.3, 7.7 seconds to travel 10 m in three trials. (a) Calculate the mean depth in cm (include the zero readings at the banks). (b) Calculate the discharge.

Students measured a river at one site. Width = 1.8 m. Depths (cm) at equal intervals from bank to bank: 0, 51, 60, 48, 26, 0. A float took 26.3, 21.9, 14.2 seconds to travel 10 m in three trials. (a) Calculate the cross-sectional area in m². (b) Calculate the discharge.

Students measured a river at one site. Width = 2.7 m. Depths (cm) at equal intervals from bank to bank: 0, 43, 49, 33, 57, 0. A float took 20.8, 8.5, 18.1 seconds to travel 10 m in three trials. (a) Calculate the mean time and then the velocity in m/s. (b) Calculate the cross-sectional area in m².
items.answer: (a) mean time 15.8 s; velocity 0.63 m/s (b) 0.819 m²

items.stem: Students in Karachi designed a questionnaire to investigate the sphere of influence of a shopping centre. They asked the first 15 people they met outside one shop at 10:00 on a Monday. Their questions included: Q3: How far have you travelled? Q1: Don’t you agree that the new shopping centre is ugly? Q5: How often do you visit? Often / Sometimes (a) Suggest an improved sampling strategy. (b) Explain why a pilot study would help.
items.answer: (a) Systematic sampling of every 10th person at several entrances, at different times on weekdays and weekends, with a sample of at least 50. (b) Testing the questionnaire on a few people would reveal unclear or leading questions before the main survey.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark method; 1 mark times/places; 1 mark size [3] (b) [2]

items.stem: Students in Kuala Lumpur designed a questionnaire to investigate the sphere of influence of a shopping centre. They asked the first 15 people they met outside one shop at 10:00 on a Monday. Their questions included: Q1: Don’t you agree that the new shopping centre is ugly? Q3: How far have you travelled? Q2: How old are you? (a) Explain why their sampling method may give biased results. (b) Explain why a pilot study would help.
items.answer: (a) Only 15 people, at one place, one time and one day: weekday morning shoppers (e.g. retired people) are over-represented; opportunistic sampling. (b) Testing the questionnaire on a few people would reveal unclear or leading questions before the main survey.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each point up to [3] (b) [2]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “choosing samples at regular intervals, for example every 10th person or every 50 m”.
items.answer: Systematic sampling
items.markingKey: Systematic sampling: choosing samples at regular intervals, for example every 10th person or every 50 m. [1]

items.stem: Explain how a questionnaire could be designed to avoid bias.
items.answer: Use clear, neutral questions; mostly closed questions with an “other” option; avoid leading questions; sample at different times and places; pilot the questionnaire.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each up to [3]

items.stem: Students want a stratified sample of 50 people (or sites) from a population divided by age group: under 18 600, 18-40 800, 41-64 2 500, 65 and over 1 400 (total 5 300). Explain how the students could choose the individuals within each group without bias.
items.answer: Use random numbers (or a systematic interval) within each group rather than choosing friends or convenient people.
items.markingKey: 1 mark method; 1 mark avoids bias [2]

items.stem: Students measured a river at one site. Width = 1.9 m. Depths (cm) at equal intervals from bank to bank: 0, 24, 8, 52, 35, 0. A float took 24.2, 17.5, 23.4 seconds to travel 10 m in three trials. (a) Calculate the mean depth in cm (include the zero readings at the banks). (b) Calculate the discharge. (c) Suggest two reasons why the float times varied. (d) Suggest one improvement to the method of measuring depth.
items.answer: (a) 19.8 cm (b) 0.174 m³/s (c) The float was caught in eddies or by vegetation; wind; different paths across the channel; reaction time with the stopwatch. (d) Take more readings at smaller intervals; use the same person to read the metre rule; read at the water surface at eye level.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a bar graph drawn on a map at the place where the data were collected”.
items.answer: Located bar graph
items.markingKey: Located bar graph: a bar graph drawn on a map at the place where the data were collected. [1]

items.stem: Explain why located bar graphs are useful for presenting fieldwork data.
items.answer: They show the values and where they were collected, so spatial patterns such as a decrease away from the CBD can be seen.
items.markingKey: 1 mark values + location; 1 mark pattern [2]

items.stem: Explain the rules for drawing an accurate graph.
items.answer: A title; labelled axes with units; a regular, suitable scale; accurately plotted points; a key if needed; neat lines or bars.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each up to [3]

items.stem: Students plan to show pedestrian counts at four sites using proportional circles. Counts: Site A 36, Site B 144, Site C 16, Site D 25. The radius (cm) will be calculated as 0.25 × √(count). Explain why the radius is calculated from the square root of the count.
items.answer: The area of a circle is proportional to the radius squared, so using the square root makes the area (what the eye sees) proportional to the count.
items.markingKey: 1 mark area ∝ r²; 1 mark area represents value [2]

items.stem: Students plan to show pedestrian counts at four sites using proportional circles. Counts: Site A 64, Site B 144, Site C 25, Site D 121. The radius (cm) will be calculated as 0.1 × √(count). (a) Calculate how many times larger the area of the largest circle is than the smallest. (b) Suggest one problem with proportional circles and how to avoid it.
items.answer: (a) 5.76 times (b) Large circles may overlap or cover the map; place them carefully, use a smaller constant, or draw them beside the map with leader lines.
items.markingKey: (a) 144 ÷ 25 [1] (b) 1 mark problem; 1 mark solution [2]

items.stem: Students plan to show pedestrian counts at four sites using proportional circles. Counts: Site A 25, Site B 169, Site C 144, Site D 49. The radius (cm) will be calculated as 0.1 × √(count). (a) Calculate the radius of each circle. (b) Suggest one problem with proportional circles and how to avoid it.
items.answer: (a) Site A 0.5 cm; Site B 1.3 cm; Site C 1.2 cm; Site D 0.7 cm (b) Large circles may overlap or cover the map; place them carefully, use a smaller constant, or draw them beside the map with leader lines.
items.markingKey: (a) 0.1 × √count for each; 1 mark for two correct, 2 for all [2] (b) 1 mark problem; 1 mark solution [2]

items.stem: Students plan to show pedestrian counts at four sites using proportional circles. Counts: Site A 144, Site B 121, Site C 64, Site D 49. The radius (cm) will be calculated as 0.2 × √(count). (a) Explain why the radius is calculated from the square root of the count. (b) Suggest one problem with proportional circles and how to avoid it.
items.answer: (a) The area of a circle is proportional to the radius squared, so using the square root makes the area (what the eye sees) proportional to the count. (b) Large circles may overlap or cover the map; place them carefully, use a smaller constant, or draw them beside the map with leader lines.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark area ∝ r²; 1 mark area represents value [2] (b) 1 mark problem; 1 mark solution [2]

items.stem: Students plan to show pedestrian counts at four sites using proportional circles. Counts: Site A 36, Site B 225, Site C 25, Site D 196. The radius (cm) will be calculated as 0.2 × √(count). (a) Calculate the radius of each circle. (b) Calculate how many times larger the area of the largest circle is than the smallest. (c) Suggest one problem with proportional circles and how to avoid it.
items.answer: (a) Site A 1.2 cm; Site B 3 cm; Site C 1 cm; Site D 2.8 cm (b) 9 times (c) Large circles may overlap or cover the map; place them carefully, use a smaller constant, or draw them beside the map with leader lines.
items.markingKey: (a) 0.2 × √count for each; 1 mark for two correct, 2 for all [2] (b) 225 ÷ 25 [1] (c) 1 mark problem; 1 mark solution [2]

items.stem: A student writes: “A line graph is suitable for data from unrelated categories such as types of shop.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Separate categories should be shown as a bar graph; a line implies continuity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: In a questionnaire, 80 shoppers answered one question. Results: car 21, bus 29, walk 7, bicycle 7, train 16. Describe how to draw the pie chart accurately.
items.answer: Draw a circle and a radius from the centre to 12 o’clock; measure each angle clockwise with a protractor, largest first; label or shade each sector with a key and add a title.
items.markingKey: 1 mark method; 1 mark labelling [2]

items.stem: In a questionnaire, 50 shoppers answered one question. Results: under 1 km 15, 1-5 km 2, 5-10 km 15, over 10 km 18. (a) Calculate the percentage for each category. (b) Calculate the angle for each sector of a pie chart.
items.markingKey: (a) count ÷ 50 × 100 [2] (b) count ÷ 50 × 360; check total 360° [2]

items.stem: Students plan to show pedestrian counts at four sites using proportional circles. Counts: Site A 64, Site B 196, Site C 16, Site D 144. The radius (cm) will be calculated as 0.2 × √(count). (a) Calculate the radius of each circle. (b) Explain why the radius is calculated from the square root of the count. (c) Suggest one problem with proportional circles and how to avoid it.
items.answer: (a) Site A 1.6 cm; Site B 2.8 cm; Site C 0.8 cm; Site D 2.4 cm (b) The area of a circle is proportional to the radius squared, so using the square root makes the area (what the eye sees) proportional to the count. (c) Large circles may overlap or cover the map; place them carefully, use a smaller constant, or draw them beside the map with leader lines.
items.markingKey: (a) 0.2 × √count for each; 1 mark for two correct, 2 for all [2] (b) 1 mark area ∝ r²; 1 mark area represents value [2] (c) 1 mark problem; 1 mark solution [2]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a summary of what the results show, stating whether the hypothesis is supported, partly supported or rejected”.
items.answer: Conclusion
items.markingKey: Conclusion: a summary of what the results show, stating whether the hypothesis is supported, partly supported or rejected. [1]

items.stem: Explain why it is important to identify anomalies in fieldwork results.
items.answer: They may be caused by errors or unusual local conditions; identifying and explaining them prevents wrong conclusions and suggests where to re-measure.
items.markingKey: 1 mark cause; 1 mark effect on conclusion [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between accuracy and reliability.
items.answer: Accuracy is how close a measurement is to the true value; reliability is whether the same results would be obtained if the investigation were repeated.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: A student tested the hypothesis “River velocity increases with distance downstream.” Results: distance downstream 1, 104; distance downstream 2, 112; distance downstream 3, 121; distance downstream 4, 136; distance downstream 5, 109; distance downstream 6, 152; distance downstream 7, 162; distance downstream 8, 164 (units: km and river velocity (m/s × 100)). Suggest two ways the student could improve the reliability of this investigation.
items.answer: Repeat the data collection on several days or times; take more readings at each site and use means; increase the number of sites; use the same equipment and person throughout.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: A student tested the hypothesis “River velocity increases with distance downstream.” Results: distance downstream 1, 110; distance downstream 2, 117; distance downstream 3, 121; distance downstream 4, 123; distance downstream 5, 129; distance downstream 6, 106; distance downstream 7, 143; distance downstream 8, 145 (units: km and river velocity (m/s × 100)). (a) Identify the anomaly and suggest a reason for it. (b) State a conclusion about the hypothesis. Use data to support your answer.
items.answer: (a) (6, 106): possibly a measurement or recording error, or a local factor (e.g. a shop entrance, tributary, path junction or groyne) at that site. (b) Largely supported: 110 at the first site and 145 at the last, apart from the anomaly.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark anomaly; 1 mark plausible reason [2] (b) 1 mark judgement; 1 mark supporting data [2]

items.stem: Students are investigating how environmental quality varies between different residential areas of Toronto. Diego’s group tested the hypothesis “Environmental quality is higher in the suburbs than in the inner city.” using an environmental quality survey (EQS) scoring litter, noise, graffiti, green space and building condition from −2 to +2. In their evaluation they note that only four sites were used and data were collected on one afternoon only. (a) Explain why the group’s conclusion may still be useful. (b) Suggest one further investigation that would extend this enquiry.
items.answer: (a) If the pattern is clear and consistent across most sites, it gives evidence about the hypothesis, especially if it agrees with theory or secondary data. (b) Repeat in a different season or place; add another variable (e.g. compare with another river/town); use secondary data to compare with past years.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark pattern evidence; 1 mark comparison with theory/secondary data [2] (b) 1 mark suggestion; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: Explain why the conclusion of a fieldwork enquiry should refer to the data.
items.answer: Quoting values, trends and anomalies provides evidence for accepting or rejecting the hypothesis and shows the strength of the relationship.
items.markingKey: 1 mark evidence; 1 mark judgement supported [2]

items.stem: A student tested the hypothesis “Pedestrian numbers decrease with distance from the centre of the CBD.” Results: distance from the CBD 1, 114; distance from the CBD 100, 102; distance from the CBD 150, 121; distance from the CBD 4, 80; distance from the CBD 250, 67; distance from the CBD 300, 58; distance from the CBD 7, 40; distance from the CBD 800, 33 (units: m and pedestrians per 10 minutes). State a conclusion about the hypothesis. Use data to support your answer.
items.answer: Largely supported: 114 at the first site and 33 at the last, apart from the anomaly.
items.markingKey: 1 mark judgement; 1 mark supporting data [2]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a question that sets out the aim of a geographical investigation”.
items.answer: Enquiry question
items.markingKey: Enquiry question: a question that sets out the aim of a geographical investigation. [1]

items.stem: Explain the value of using both primary and secondary data in an investigation.
items.answer: Primary data is specific to the hypothesis and up to date; secondary data gives context, a wider area or change over time and can be used to check primary results.
items.markingKey: 1 mark primary; 1 mark secondary [2]

items.stem: Students are investigating how beach sediment changes along a beach affected by longshore drift near Auckland. Describe a method of collecting primary data to test the hypothesis.
items.answer: Measuring the long axis of 10 pebbles at each site with callipers and classifying roundness using a Powers scale.
items.markingKey: 1 mark method; 1 mark detail (how/where/when) [2]

items.stem: Students are investigating how microclimate varies around their school in Jakarta. Freya’s group has one day for fieldwork and their hypothesis is “Temperature is higher and wind speed lower in sheltered sites close to buildings.” (a) Explain why a pilot study would be useful. (b) Explain how the group could make sure their results are reliable.
items.answer: (a) To check that methods work, that questions or recording sheets are clear, and how long each site takes, so the day is used efficiently. (b) Repeat measurements and take means, use the same equipment and times at each site, use a large enough sample, and have the same person record each measurement.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each up to [2] (b) 1 mark each up to [3]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “dividing the population into groups and sampling each group in proportion to its size”.
items.answer: Stratified sampling
items.markingKey: Stratified sampling: dividing the population into groups and sampling each group in proportion to its size. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “Opportunistic sampling is the least biased method.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. It only includes people or places that are convenient, so it is often the most biased.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain why the velocity of a river should be measured more than once at each site.
items.answer: Floats can be caught by obstacles or wind, so repeating three times and taking the mean reduces the effect of anomalies and improves reliability.
items.markingKey: 1 mark reason; 1 mark mean/reliability [2]

items.stem: Students counted pedestrians for 15 minutes at five sites along a transect away from the centre of Cairo: Site 1 79, Site 2 73, Site 3 60, Site 4 42, Site 5 39. Suggest why the count should be repeated at different times of day.
items.answer: Pedestrian numbers vary (e.g. lunchtime peaks), so repeating gives a fairer, more representative picture.

items.stem: Students want a stratified sample of 50 people (or sites) from a population divided by land use type: woodland 4 000, farmland 500, urban 3 800, water 1 900 (total 10 200). (a) Explain why stratified sampling is suitable here. (b) Suggest one problem the students may face in collecting this sample.
items.answer: (a) Each group is represented in proportion to its size, so the sample is more representative than random or opportunistic sampling. (b) People may refuse to answer; some groups are harder to find at certain times; time constraints.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark proportional; 1 mark representative [2] (b) [1]

items.stem: Students want a stratified sample of 40 people (or sites) from a population divided by land use type: woodland 2 000, farmland 1 600, urban 2 600, water 2 300 (total 8 500). (a) Explain why stratified sampling is suitable here. (b) Explain how the students could choose the individuals within each group without bias. (c) Suggest one problem the students may face in collecting this sample.
items.answer: (a) Each group is represented in proportion to its size, so the sample is more representative than random or opportunistic sampling. (b) Use random numbers (or a systematic interval) within each group rather than choosing friends or convenient people. (c) People may refuse to answer; some groups are harder to find at certain times; time constraints.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark proportional; 1 mark representative [2] (b) 1 mark method; 1 mark avoids bias [2] (c) [1]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “located bar graph”?
options: A map with lines joining places of equal value, such as temperature or pedestrian numbers.
A bar graph drawn on a map at the place where the data were collected.
A map with straight lines drawn from the origin to the destination of journeys.
Circles drawn on a map whose areas are proportional to the values they represent.
items.answer: A bar graph drawn on a map at the place where the data were collected.
items.markingKey: Located bar graph: a bar graph drawn on a map at the place where the data were collected. [1]

items.stem: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of proportional circles.
items.answer: Advantage: show size and location clearly. Disadvantage: large circles can overlap and hide others, and areas are hard to compare accurately by eye.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Students plan to show pedestrian counts at four sites using proportional circles. Counts: Site A 16, Site B 196, Site C 144, Site D 121. The radius (cm) will be calculated as 0.25 × √(count). Suggest one problem with proportional circles and how to avoid it.
items.answer: Large circles may overlap or cover the map; place them carefully, use a smaller constant, or draw them beside the map with leader lines.
items.markingKey: 1 mark problem; 1 mark solution [2]

items.stem: In a questionnaire, 60 shoppers answered one question. Results: food 34, clothes 1, services 5, leisure 20. Calculate the percentage for each category.
items.answer: food 56.7%; clothes 1.7%; services 8.3%; leisure 33.3%

items.stem: Students plan to show pedestrian counts at four sites using proportional circles. Counts: Site A 64, Site B 144, Site C 121, Site D 169. The radius (cm) will be calculated as 0.1 × √(count). (a) Explain why the radius is calculated from the square root of the count. (b) Calculate how many times larger the area of the largest circle is than the smallest.
items.answer: (a) The area of a circle is proportional to the radius squared, so using the square root makes the area (what the eye sees) proportional to the count. (b) 2.64 times
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark area ∝ r²; 1 mark area represents value [2] (b) 169 ÷ 64 [1]

items.stem: In a questionnaire, 80 shoppers answered one question. Results: car 12, bus 14, walk 10, bicycle 43, train 1. (a) Calculate the angle for each sector of a pie chart. (b) Describe how to draw the pie chart accurately. (c) Suggest an alternative way of presenting these results.
items.answer: (a) car 54°; bus 63°; walk 45°; bicycle 193.5°; train 4.5° (b) Draw a circle and a radius from the centre to 12 o’clock; measure each angle clockwise with a protractor, largest first; label or shade each sector with a key and add a title. (c) A bar graph or divided bar graph, which is easier to draw and compare accurately.
items.markingKey: (a) count ÷ 80 × 360; check total 360° [2] (b) 1 mark method; 1 mark labelling [2] (c) 1 mark technique; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: A student writes: “A strong correlation proves that one variable causes the other.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Correlation shows a relationship; another factor could cause both.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain how the sample size can affect the conclusion of an enquiry.
items.answer: A small sample may be unrepresentative and easily distorted by anomalies, so the conclusion is less reliable; a larger sample gives more confidence.
items.markingKey: 1 mark small sample problem; 1 mark larger sample benefit [2]

items.stem: A student calculated Spearman’s rank correlation for distance from source (km) (X) and channel width (dm) (Y) at 6 sites: X 25, Y 103; X 20, Y 97; X 7, Y 76; X 37, Y 131; X 23, Y 86; X 33, Y 112. Calculate rs using rs = 1 − 6Σd² ÷ (n³ − n).

Students are investigating the sphere of influence of a shopping centre in Lima. Yusuf’s group tested the hypothesis “Most shoppers travel less than 5 km to the shopping centre.” using a questionnaire asking shoppers where they have travelled from, how they travelled and how often they visit. In their evaluation they note that a sample of 12 people was used and data were collected on one afternoon only. (a) Explain how each of these limitations may have affected the results. (b) Explain why the group’s conclusion may still be useful.
items.answer: (a) Because a sample of 12 people was used, the results may not be representative or consistent, which reduces reliability. Because data were collected on one afternoon only, the results may not be representative or consistent, which reduces reliability. (b) If the pattern is clear and consistent across most sites, it gives evidence about the hypothesis, especially if it agrees with theory or secondary data.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each limitation explained [2] (b) 1 mark pattern evidence; 1 mark comparison with theory/secondary data [2]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “data collected first-hand in the field by the investigator”.
items.answer: Primary data
items.markingKey: Primary data: data collected first-hand in the field by the investigator. [1]

items.stem: Explain why it is important to collect data at the same time of day at each site.
items.answer: Conditions such as pedestrian numbers, traffic or temperature change through the day, so collecting at the same time makes the results fair and comparable.
items.markingKey: 1 mark conditions vary; 1 mark fair comparison [2]

items.stem: Students are investigating the sphere of influence of a shopping centre in Karachi. Describe and justify a suitable sampling strategy.
items.answer: Systematic sampling: asking every 10th person who passes, at different times of day, which gives an even, unbiased spread of data that can be compared.
items.markingKey: 1 mark strategy; 1 mark justification [2]

items.stem: Students are investigating how traffic flow varies during the day on a main road in Dhaka. Ethan’s group has one day for fieldwork and their hypothesis is “Traffic flow is highest during the morning and evening rush hours.” (a) Explain why a pilot study would be useful. (b) Explain how the group could make sure their results are reliable.
items.answer: (a) To check that methods work, that questions or recording sheets are clear, and how long each site takes, so the day is used efficiently. (b) Repeat measurements and take means, use the same equipment and times at each site, use a large enough sample, and have the same person record each measurement.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each up to [2] (b) 1 mark each up to [3]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “choosing people or sites that are convenient or willing to take part”.
items.answer: Opportunistic sampling
items.markingKey: Opportunistic sampling: choosing people or sites that are convenient or willing to take part. [1]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Taking more readings at each site generally improves reliability.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Means of repeated readings reduce the effect of errors and anomalies.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why the velocity of a river should be measured more than once at each site. (b) A student writes: “Opportunistic sampling is the least biased method.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Floats can be caught by obstacles or wind, so repeating three times and taking the mean reduces the effect of anomalies and improves reliability. (b) Not correct. It only includes people or places that are convenient, so it is often the most biased.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark reason; 1 mark mean/reliability [2] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Students measured a river at one site. Width = 4.9 m. Depths (cm) at equal intervals from bank to bank: 0, 38, 30, 46, 0. A float took 22.2, 11.9, 13.1 seconds to travel 10 m in three trials. Suggest two reasons why the float times varied.
items.answer: The float was caught in eddies or by vegetation; wind; different paths across the channel; reaction time with the stopwatch.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Students counted pedestrians for 5 minutes at five sites along a transect away from the centre of Mexico City: Site 1 85, Site 2 53, Site 3 26, Site 4 22, Site 5 9. (a) Calculate the mean count per site. (b) Suggest why the count should be repeated at different times of day.
items.answer: (a) 39 (b) Pedestrian numbers vary (e.g. lunchtime peaks), so repeating gives a fairer, more representative picture.

items.stem: Students in Seoul designed a questionnaire to investigate the sphere of influence of a shopping centre. They asked the first 15 people they met outside one shop at 10:00 on a Monday. Their questions included: Q3: How far have you travelled? Q1: Don’t you agree that the new shopping centre is ugly? Q2: How old are you? (a) Suggest an improved sampling strategy. (b) Explain why a pilot study would help.
items.answer: (a) Systematic sampling of every 10th person at several entrances, at different times on weekdays and weekends, with a sample of at least 50. (b) Testing the questionnaire on a few people would reveal unclear or leading questions before the main survey.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark method; 1 mark times/places; 1 mark size [3] (b) [2]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “proportional circles”?
options: A graph that shows each value as a dot along a scale, showing the spread of the data.
Circles drawn on a map whose areas are proportional to the values they represent.
A map with straight lines drawn from the origin to the destination of journeys.
A map with lines joining places of equal value, such as temperature or pedestrian numbers.
items.answer: Circles drawn on a map whose areas are proportional to the values they represent.
items.markingKey: Proportional circles: circles drawn on a map whose areas are proportional to the values they represent. [1]

items.stem: Explain why it is helpful to use more than one presentation technique.
items.answer: Different techniques show different things – a map shows location and pattern, a scatter graph shows relationship – so together they give a fuller picture.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Students plan to show pedestrian counts at four sites using proportional circles. Counts: Site A 49, Site B 36, Site C 64, Site D 169. The radius (cm) will be calculated as 0.25 × √(count). Suggest one problem with proportional circles and how to avoid it.
items.answer: Large circles may overlap or cover the map; place them carefully, use a smaller constant, or draw them beside the map with leader lines.
items.markingKey: 1 mark problem; 1 mark solution [2]

items.stem: In a questionnaire, 60 shoppers answered one question. Results: food 4, clothes 1, services 46, leisure 9. Calculate the percentage for each category.
items.answer: food 6.7%; clothes 1.7%; services 76.7%; leisure 15%

items.stem: Students plan to show pedestrian counts at four sites using proportional circles. Counts: Site A 169, Site B 64, Site C 121, Site D 144. The radius (cm) will be calculated as 0.25 × √(count). (a) Explain why the radius is calculated from the square root of the count. (b) Calculate how many times larger the area of the largest circle is than the smallest.
items.answer: (a) The area of a circle is proportional to the radius squared, so using the square root makes the area (what the eye sees) proportional to the count. (b) 2.64 times
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark area ∝ r²; 1 mark area represents value [2] (b) 169 ÷ 64 [1]

items.stem: Students plan to show pedestrian counts at four sites using proportional circles. Counts: Site A 121, Site B 169, Site C 225, Site D 16. The radius (cm) will be calculated as 0.25 × √(count). (a) Calculate the radius of each circle. (b) Explain why the radius is calculated from the square root of the count. (c) Suggest one problem with proportional circles and how to avoid it.
items.answer: (a) Site A 2.75 cm; Site B 3.25 cm; Site C 3.75 cm; Site D 1 cm (b) The area of a circle is proportional to the radius squared, so using the square root makes the area (what the eye sees) proportional to the count. (c) Large circles may overlap or cover the map; place them carefully, use a smaller constant, or draw them beside the map with leader lines.
items.markingKey: (a) 0.25 × √count for each; 1 mark for two correct, 2 for all [2] (b) 1 mark area ∝ r²; 1 mark area represents value [2] (c) 1 mark problem; 1 mark solution [2]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Evaluation should include suggestions for improving the investigation.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Improvements to methods, sampling and timing show understanding of the limitations.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: A revision website states: “If a result does not fit the pattern it should always be deleted.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Anomalies should be checked and explained; deleting them without reason can bias the conclusion.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: A student tested the hypothesis “River velocity increases with distance downstream.” Results: distance downstream 1, 102; distance downstream 2, 114; distance downstream 3, 120; distance downstream 4, 136; distance downstream 5, 150; distance downstream 6, 158; distance downstream 7, 147; distance downstream 8, 182 (units: km and river velocity (m/s × 100)). Suggest two ways the student could improve the reliability of this investigation.
items.answer: Repeat the data collection on several days or times; take more readings at each site and use means; increase the number of sites; use the same equipment and person throughout.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Students are investigating whether pedestrian numbers decrease with distance from the centre of the CBD of Hanoi. Aisha’s group tested the hypothesis “Pedestrian numbers decrease with distance from the centre of the CBD.” using counting pedestrians passing a point for 10 minutes at each site and recording the time. In their evaluation they note that it rained heavily during the second half of the day and a sample of 12 people was used. (a) Explain how each of these limitations may have affected the results. (b) Explain why the group’s conclusion may still be useful.
items.answer: (a) Because it rained heavily during the second half of the day, the results may not be representative or consistent, which reduces reliability. Because a sample of 12 people was used, the results may not be representative or consistent, which reduces reliability. (b) If the pattern is clear and consistent across most sites, it gives evidence about the hypothesis, especially if it agrees with theory or secondary data.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each limitation explained [2] (b) 1 mark pattern evidence; 1 mark comparison with theory/secondary data [2]
